title: AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship & Growth
blurb: Beyond the launch: AI-native market research, operations automation, fundraising and pitch materials, growth engines, and an AI-leveraged operating model for founders scaling past themselves. (Launching from zero? Start with AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship.)

modules.d: Running a growing business with AI as a force multiplier — without losing judgement, voice or integrity.
modules.body:
Beyond the launch

Launching a business proves you can sell. Growing it proves you can build a system: repeatable sales, reliable operations, healthy cash flow and a team or partners. AI changes how small businesses scale. Tasks that once required hiring — copywriting, basic analysis, customer response drafting, research, bookkeeping support — can now be handled by a founder with well-designed AI workflows. The AI-native founder designs the business so that AI handles the repetitive work and humans focus on customers, strategy, relationships and quality.

The founder's time audit

Growth usually stalls because the founder is the bottleneck: answering every message, making every design, chasing every payment. Track your time for one week in categories: selling, delivering, customer service, marketing, administration and finance, learning and strategy. Then mark each activity: automate (rule-based, repetitive), AI-assist (needs judgement but benefits from drafts), delegate (someone else could do it with a procedure), or keep (needs you — key relationships, strategy, final quality). Most founders find 30–50% of their week falls into the first three categories.

The leverage principle. Your goal is not to do more work faster; it is to multiply the impact of each hour. An hour building a reusable template, automation or procedure that saves ten minutes a day returns about 60 hours a year. Prioritise leverage over effort.

Where AI multiplies a growing business

  • Sales: personalised follow-up drafts, proposal templates, objection-handling scripts.
  • Marketing: content calendars, repurposing one piece of content into many formats, campaign analysis.
  • Customer service: FAQ answers, response templates, summarising feedback.
  • Operations: standard operating procedures (SOPs), checklists, supplier communication.
  • Finance: spreadsheet formulas, cash flow forecasts, pricing scenarios, invoice reminders.
  • Strategy: market scans, competitor summaries, scenario analysis and decision support.

What must stay human

Key customer relationships, negotiations, hiring decisions, final quality checks, ethical judgements and the founder's vision cannot be outsourced to AI. Customers can tell when they are treated as a process. Use AI to create more time for the human moments that build loyalty.

Risks of the AI-native business

  • Generic voice: AI content that sounds like everyone else erodes your brand.
  • Errors at scale: an automated message with a wrong price reaches every customer at once.
  • Data exposure: customer and financial data shared with tools without understanding their terms.
  • Tool dependency: building processes on a single tool that changes pricing or features.
  • Skill erosion: founders who stop understanding their own numbers or customers.

The founder's AI operating rhythm

Successful founders build a weekly rhythm: Monday planning (priorities and content), daily customer and sales blocks, a weekly review of numbers (revenue, cash, pipeline, customer feedback), and a monthly improvement session to automate or refine one process. AI supports each step; the founder owns the decisions.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my business operations coach. Ask me to list my typical weekly activities and hours. Classify each as automate, AI-assist, delegate or keep, estimate hours I could free each week, and rank the top five leverage opportunities by hours saved and ease. Then propose a weekly operating rhythm for me as an AI-native founder.

Going deeper — the leverage stack and your first 30 days

The time audit tells you where your hours go; the next step is to decide in what order to build leverage. A useful framework is the leverage stack, built from the bottom up: (1) eliminate work that creates no value for customers; (2) simplify what remains into a clear sequence of steps; (3) standardise it as a written procedure or template; (4) automate the rule-based parts; and (5) AI-assist the parts that need judgement but benefit from a draft. Founders often jump straight to step 4 or 5 and end up automating confusion. If a process cannot be explained in a short checklist, it is not ready for automation.

Prioritising candidates. Score each task on three dimensions from 1 to 5: frequency (how often it occurs), time per occurrence, and risk if done wrong. Start with high-frequency, moderate-time, low-risk tasks — for example drafting replies to common customer questions — and keep high-risk tasks such as pricing decisions, contracts or sensitive customer complaints firmly in the "keep" or "AI-assist with review" categories.

Worked example. A tailor in Bafoussam spends roughly an hour a day replying to WhatsApp messages about prices, delivery times and fabric choices. Eliminate: stop sending individual photos of every fabric — publish one catalogue. Simplify: group questions into five types. Standardise: write five reply templates. AI-assist: use an AI tool to draft personalised replies from the templates, which the tailor checks before sending. Keep: final price negotiation with large orders. The tailor tracks minutes per day for two weeks to see whether the change actually saves time.

The founder's operating rhythm. Leverage also comes from routines: a weekly 30-minute review of key numbers, a monthly review of which templates and AI prompts need updating, and a quarterly decision on what to delegate next. An AI assistant can help prepare these reviews — summarising the week's sales notes or customer feedback — but the decisions remain yours.

Pitfalls. Building tools instead of serving customers; adopting many apps that do not connect; letting AI-generated messages sound generic so loyal customers feel ignored; and forgetting that customer data shared with AI tools must be handled lawfully and with care. Check your country's data protection rules — for example Cameroon's and those of any market you sell into — before uploading customer lists.

Your first 30 days. Week 1: time audit. Week 2: pick two tasks and work through the leverage stack. Week 3: run the new process and measure. Week 4: keep what worked, drop what did not, and choose the next two tasks.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my operations coach. Here is a list of tasks from my one-week time audit with approximate minutes per week: [paste]. Score each task for frequency, time and risk; place it in the leverage stack (eliminate, simplify, standardise, automate, AI-assist, keep); and recommend the two tasks I should tackle first. For each, draft a simple checklist procedure and tell me how to measure whether the change saved time.

📚 Glossary

  • AI-native founder: founder who designs the business around AI-supported workflows
  • Time audit: tracking where working hours actually go
  • Leverage: multiplying impact per hour through systems
  • SOP: standard operating procedure
  • Operating rhythm: regular cadence of planning, execution and review

📖 References

  • Gerber, M. (1995). The E-Myth Revisited.
  • Mollick, E. (2024). Co-Intelligence.
  • Forteh, I. (2026). AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship. Team21 Academy.

quiz.q: Claudine, who runs a Douala catering firm, spends 6 hours a week writing similar quotes for event clients. Each quote needs her judgement on menu and pricing. How should she classify this work in the time audit?
opts: Keep, because any client-facing document must be written by the founder herself
Automate, because quoting is a routine task that repeats every single week
AI-assist, since she still decides while a tool prepares the first version
Delegate, because a junior staff member could price menus without guidance
quiz.x: AI-assist fits tasks that need judgement but benefit from drafts. Automate suits rule-based work; quotes here need her pricing judgement, so full automation is the runner-up but wrong.

quiz.q: Moses builds a reusable proposal template in 2 hours that saves him 15 minutes a day, 5 days a week, for 48 weeks a year. Roughly how many hours does it return in a year?
opts: About 60 hours, since 15 minutes x 5 days x 48 weeks = 3,600 minutes
About 90 hours, since 15 minutes x 7 days x 52 weeks is roughly 5,460
About 30 hours, since 15 minutes x 5 days x 48 weeks = 1,800 minutes
About 12 hours, since 15 minutes x 48 weeks is about 720 minutes total
quiz.x: 15 x 5 x 48 = 3,600 minutes = 60 hours, minus 2 hours to build. The 90-hour option wrongly assumes 7 days and 52 weeks.

quiz.q: A Nairobi e-commerce founder sets up an automated WhatsApp message announcing a price. A typo lists 5,000 instead of 50,000, and it reaches 2,000 customers at once. Which AI-native risk is this?
opts: Tool dependency, because the business relies on one messaging tool
Errors at scale, because one mistake reaches every customer at once
Generic voice, because automated messages sound like every competitor
Skill erosion, because the founder no longer understands her numbers
quiz.x: The module defines errors at scale as an automated wrong price reaching every customer. Tool dependency concerns pricing or feature changes by a vendor.

quiz.q: Rodrigue, a Yaoundé founder, wants to hand three tasks to AI: drafting FAQ replies, negotiating a supplier contract, and summarising weekly feedback. Which should stay with him?
opts: Summarising weekly feedback, since it shapes strategic choices later
Drafting FAQ replies, since customers can tell when replies are generic
None of them need him, since AI can complete each with good prompts
Negotiating the supplier contract, since negotiations stay human-led
quiz.x: Negotiations, key relationships, hiring and final quality checks stay human. AI can summarise feedback and draft FAQ replies, which he reviews.

quiz.q: After a year of relying on AI dashboards, Sandrine cannot explain her gross margin when a bank officer asks. Which risk from the module has she fallen into?
opts: Generic voice, since the AI reports used standard wording throughout
Data exposure, since dashboards shared her figures with third parties
Errors at scale, since the dashboard may have miscalculated a figure
Skill erosion, since she has stopped understanding her own numbers
quiz.x: Skill erosion is founders who stop understanding their own numbers or customers. Errors at scale might also occur, but the described symptom is her lost understanding.

quiz.q: A Boston bakery owner tracks a week: 10 h selling, 12 h delivering, 8 h customer messages, 6 h admin, 4 h strategy. She marks messages and admin as AI-assist or automate. What share of her 40 hours is that?
opts: 35%, since 14 hours out of 40 hours equals thirty-five percent
45%, since admin, messages and strategy add up to 18 hours
20%, since 8 hours of messages is a fifth of her working week
30%, since 12 hours of delivery work is the largest category
quiz.x: 8 + 6 = 14 hours; 14 / 40 = 35%, within the 30-50% range the module says most founders find.

quiz.q: Which weekly operating rhythm best matches the module for an AI-native founder of a small Bafoussam printing business?
opts: Daily planning, weekly sales blocks, quarterly review, yearly automation sprint
Monday sales blocks, weekly AI content batch, monthly plan, no number reviews
Monday planning, daily sales blocks, weekly numbers review, monthly process fix
Daily AI reports reviewed by staff, and the founder reviewing results yearly
quiz.x: The module's rhythm: Monday planning, daily customer and sales blocks, a weekly numbers review and a monthly improvement session. The others drop the weekly review.

quiz.q: Ali's growth has stalled: he answers every WhatsApp message himself and designs every flyer. What does the module suggest is the first step to fix this?
opts: Buy a premium AI subscription and let it reply to every customer message
Do a one-week time audit and classify tasks as automate, assist, delegate, keep
Raise prices so fewer customers write, which reduces the daily volume of messages
Hire two assistants straight away so that he can step back from operations
quiz.x: The time audit reveals where hours go before choosing what to automate, AI-assist or delegate. Hiring immediately may be useful later but skips the diagnosis.

quiz.q: A founder builds her whole order process on one free automation tool. The provider then triples its price. Which risk does this show, and what is a sensible mitigation?
opts: Skill erosion; take a course in spreadsheet formulas to keep sharp
Generic voice; rewrite customer messages in her own personal style
Data exposure; encrypt every spreadsheet that the tool can access
Tool dependency; document the process so it can move to another tool
quiz.x: Tool dependency is reliance on a single tool that changes pricing or features; documenting the process (an SOP) eases switching.

quiz.q: Two founders in Accra compare AI use. Kwame uses AI to answer complaints automatically with no review. Efua uses AI to draft replies and personally handles refunds and sensitive cases. Whose approach fits the module?
opts: Both equally, since each uses AI to cut the hours spent on customer service
Kwame's, since customers rarely notice whether a person wrote the reply
Efua's, since sensitive moments stay human while AI drafts routine replies
Kwame's, since automatic replies cut response times for every complaint
quiz.x: Customers can tell when treated as a process; AI should create time for human moments. Kwame's speed gain is real but sacrifices loyalty in sensitive cases.

facts.t: Share of a founder's week that typically falls into automate, AI-assist or delegate.
facts.more: A one-week time audit usually reveals that much of the week does not need the founder personally — that time can move to customers and strategy.

facts.t: Yearly return on a template that saves 10 minutes a day.
facts.more: 10 minutes × 365 days ≈ 61 hours. One hour of building is leverage; doing the same task faster every day is only effort.

facts.t: Automate, AI-assist, delegate, keep.
facts.more: Rule-based repetition is automated; judgement-heavy drafting is AI-assisted; procedures go to others; relationships, strategy and final quality stay with you.

facts.t: The E-Myth Revisited: work ON the business, not just IN it.
facts.more: Michael Gerber argued small businesses stall when the owner is the system. SOPs and AI workflows are modern versions of his advice.

modules.d: Sizing markets, mapping competitors and reading customers — ethically and with evidence.
modules.body:
Growth needs a map

To grow beyond your first customers, you need to know how big the opportunity is, who else is competing for it, and what customers value. Market and competitive intelligence turns guesses into evidence-based choices about where to expand, what to offer and how to position.

Sizing the market: TAM, SAM, SOM

TAM (total addressable market) is the total demand for a product category. SAM (serviceable available market) is the part you can serve with your business model, geography and channels. SOM (serviceable obtainable market) is the share you can realistically win in the next few years. Investors distrust giant top-down numbers ("Africa has 1.4 billion people, if we get 1%…"). Stronger is bottom-up sizing: number of target customers × likelihood of purchase × price × purchase frequency.

Bottom-up example. A school-lunch delivery service in one Yaoundé district: 12 private schools × average 250 pupils = 3,000 pupils. If 10% subscribe at 15,000 CFA per month for 9 school months: 300 × 15,000 × 9 = 40.5 million CFA per year SOM in that district. Each assumption — schools, pupils, uptake, price — can be tested through conversations and pilots.

Competitive analysis

Map direct competitors (same solution), indirect competitors (different solutions to the same problem) and substitutes (including doing nothing or doing it yourself). For each, examine offer, price, quality, channels, customer reviews, strengths and weaknesses. A positioning map plots competitors on two dimensions customers care about — for example price and speed — revealing empty spaces you could occupy.

Porter's five forces help assess industry attractiveness: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of buyers, and bargaining power of suppliers. Industries with low barriers to entry, such as many digital services, need differentiation and loyalty to protect margins.

Reading customers at scale

Customer reviews, comments and messages are a free source of intelligence. AI can analyse hundreds of reviews of your business and competitors to identify recurring praise and complaints — "late delivery", "friendly staff", "prices unclear". These themes reveal unmet needs and opportunities for differentiation. Combine with direct interviews and surveys, and track the jobs to be done: the progress customers are trying to make in their lives, which explains why they choose one solution over another.

Using AI for research — carefully

AI can summarise industry reports, suggest competitor categories, structure analyses and draft survey questions. But AI may invent statistics or describe outdated or non-existent competitors, especially in local markets. Use AI to generate hypotheses and frameworks; verify facts through primary research (visits, mystery shopping, interviews) and reliable secondary sources (national statistics, industry associations, reputable reports).

Ethical intelligence

Gather intelligence from public information, customers who choose to talk, and your own observation. Do not lie about your identity to obtain confidential information, induce competitors' employees to share secrets, or copy protected materials. Ethical intelligence protects your reputation and avoids legal risk.

From insight to action

Intelligence is valuable only if it changes decisions: which segment to target next, which feature to add, what price to charge, which message to emphasise. End every analysis with two or three concrete decisions.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my market intelligence analyst. For my [business] in [city/country], help me build a bottom-up SOM estimate with explicit assumptions I can test, a competitor map of direct, indirect and substitute options, and a two-axis positioning map. Then analyse the customer reviews I paste (mine and competitors') for recurring themes and end with three concrete decisions. Mark every fact I must verify locally.

📚 Glossary

  • TAM / SAM / SOM: total, serviceable and obtainable market
  • Bottom-up sizing: building market estimates from customer-level assumptions
  • Positioning map: visual comparison of competitors on two key dimensions
  • Jobs to be done: the progress customers seek when choosing a product
  • Substitute: a different way of meeting the same need

📖 References

  • Porter, M. (2008). The five competitive forces that shape strategy. Harvard Business Review.
  • Christensen, C. et al. (2016). Know your customers' 'jobs to be done'. Harvard Business Review.
  • Strategic and Competitive Intelligence Professionals (SCIP) — Code of Ethics.

quiz.q: A Yaoundé school-lunch service targets 12 private schools averaging 250 pupils. It assumes 10% subscribe at 15,000 CFA per month for 9 school months. What is the bottom-up SOM per year?
opts: 40.5 million CFA, since 300 x 15,000 x 9 months
54 million CFA, since 300 x 15,000 x 12 months
405 million CFA, since 3,000 x 15,000 x 9 months
4.5 million CFA, since 300 x 15,000 = 4.5 million
quiz.x: 3,000 pupils x 10% = 300; 300 x 15,000 x 9 = 40.5 million CFA. Using 12 months ignores the school year; omitting uptake gives 405 million.

quiz.q: A startup pitch says: 'Africa has 1.4 billion people; if we capture 1%, we have 14 million customers.' Why do investors distrust this, according to the module?
opts: It covers Africa rather than one country, which investors prefer
It is top-down and untested, unlike customer-level bottom-up sizing
It uses too small a market share, as serious pitches assume 10%
It counts customers instead of revenue, which is the usual measure
quiz.x: Investors distrust giant top-down numbers; bottom-up sizing builds from testable customer-level assumptions.

quiz.q: A Douala taxi-moto delivery startup lists rivals: another moto delivery app, customers' own relatives who run errands, and shop owners who deliver themselves. How should 'relatives who run errands' be classified?
opts: As a non-competitor, since relatives do not charge any money
As a key partner, since relatives could join the courier fleet
As a substitute, since it means customers doing it themselves
As a direct competitor, since relatives deliver the same parcels
quiz.x: Substitutes include doing it yourself or doing nothing. Direct competitors offer the same solution as a business.

quiz.q: A US craft-coffee founder wants to find an empty space in her city's market. Which tool from the module plots competitors on two dimensions customers care about?
opts: A bottom-up SOM estimate built from customer-level assumptions
A Porter's five forces assessment of the local coffee industry
A jobs-to-be-done interview guide for regular coffee buyers
A positioning map, for example on price against speed of service
quiz.x: A positioning map plots competitors on two dimensions to reveal gaps. Five forces assesses industry attractiveness, not specific gaps.

quiz.q: Ngozi asks an AI to list competitors for her Bamenda tailoring shop. It names five businesses, two of which she has never heard of. What is the best next step?
opts: Verify them through visits, calls or reliable local sources
Ask the AI again and keep the names that appear both times
Add all five to her competitor map, since AI uses online data
Drop AI research and rely on her own impressions instead
quiz.x: AI may invent or describe outdated competitors in local markets; verify through primary research. Repeating the prompt does not verify anything.

quiz.q: A digital-design agency in Buea faces dozens of new freelancers each month with almost no start-up cost. Under Porter's five forces, what does the module say such firms need?
opts: A larger office, since physical presence deters new freelancers
Differentiation and loyalty to protect margins from new entrants
Lower prices than every new entrant to block them from the market
More suppliers, since supplier power drives most digital rivalry
quiz.x: Low barriers to entry mean a high threat of new entrants; differentiation and loyalty protect margins. Price-cutting erodes margins further.

quiz.q: Analysing 300 reviews of local salons, an AI finds 'prices unclear' is the most frequent complaint. What should Mireille, a salon owner, do with this insight?
opts: Note it in a report and revisit the analysis again next year
Decide to publish a clear price list and test its effect on bookings
Lower all her prices, since unclear pricing usually means prices are too high
Share the reviews with competitors to improve the whole sector
quiz.x: Intelligence is valuable only if it changes decisions; end every analysis with concrete decisions. Lowering prices misreads the complaint.

quiz.q: To learn a rival's supplier prices, Joel considers posing as a buyer from a large hotel chain to get confidential quotes. What does the module say?
opts: Unethical, but legal, so it is a personal judgement for Joel
Acceptable, since supplier quotes are ordinary commercial data, not secrets
Acceptable, if he later shares useful findings with his staff
Unethical, since lying about identity breaches ethical intelligence
quiz.x: Do not lie about your identity to obtain confidential information; it risks reputation and legal trouble.

quiz.q: A parent picks an evening tutoring service not for grades but to free time for her evening job. In the module's terms, what is this?
opts: The job to be done: the progress the parent seeks in her life
The total addressable market for tutoring across the whole city
A threat of new entrants into the evening tutoring industry
A substitute product that competes with private school fees
quiz.x: Jobs to be done is the progress customers try to make, explaining why they choose a solution. This parent's job is freeing evening time.

quiz.q: A Lagos pharmacy chain estimates SOM for a delivery service: 8,000 households, 5% uptake, 3,000 NGN per order, 4 orders per month. What is the monthly SOM?
opts: 96 million NGN, since 8,000 x 3,000 x 4 orders
1.2 million NGN, since 400 x 3,000 per month
4.8 million NGN, since 400 x 3,000 x 4 orders
57.6 million NGN, since 400 x 3,000 x 4 x 12
quiz.x: 8,000 x 5% = 400; 400 x 3,000 x 4 = 4.8 million NGN per month. The 57.6 million figure is annual, not monthly.

facts.t: Bottom-up SOM for school-lunch delivery in one Yaoundé district.
facts.more: 12 schools × 250 pupils × 10% uptake × 15,000 CFA × 9 months. Every assumption can be tested in conversations and a pilot — unlike 'if we get 1% of Africa'.

facts.t: Porter: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer and supplier power.
facts.more: Low entry barriers, common in digital services, mean differentiation and loyalty must protect margins.

facts.t: Total, serviceable, obtainable — each is a subset of the last.
facts.more: Investors care most about SOM: what you can realistically win in the next few years with your model, geography and channels.

facts.t: Direct competitors, indirect competitors, substitutes.
facts.more: For many small businesses the biggest competitor is 'doing nothing' or 'doing it yourself' — a substitute that never appears in a list of companies.

labs.title: Audit this AI market report
labs.intro: A founder asked AI for a market brief on laundry pick-up in Buea. Tap every line you must not use without verification or correction.
segments: Buea's student population creates steady demand for laundry services,
and the market is worth exactly 2.3 billion CFA per year according to the National Institute of Statistics.
Precise figure with an official-sounding source — classic AI fabrication. Check the actual INS publication.
Your main competitor, CleanFast Buea, charges 500 CFA per kilo.
AI may invent or outdate local competitors. Verify by visiting or mystery shopping.
Substitutes include washing at home and paying neighbours informally.
A bottom-up estimate should start from the number of students in rented rooms near campus,
multiplied by the share who already pay for laundry and the price per load.
To learn rivals' margins, call them pretending to be a supplier.
Lying about identity to get confidential information is unethical and a legal and reputation risk.
Reading public reviews of competitors can reveal recurring complaints such as late returns.
labs.tip: Use AI for frameworks and hypotheses; verify facts through primary research and reliable sources, ethically.

plaibox.intro: Start with the school-lunch example, then replace each assumption with your own market's numbers.

modules.d: Systems for sales, orders, customer service, finance and inventory — designed for reliability.
modules.body:
Operations are what customers actually experience

Marketing brings customers once; operations decide whether they return. Late deliveries, lost orders, inconsistent quality or slow responses destroy growth. As volume grows, informal processes that worked for ten customers collapse at a hundred. An operations stack — documented processes supported by simple tools and automation — keeps quality consistent as you grow.

Start with processes, not tools

Map your core processes from the customer's point of view: inquiry → quote → order → payment → delivery → follow-up. For each step, define who does what, the standard, the time target and the information needed. Write it as a standard operating procedure (SOP): a short checklist someone else could follow. AI drafts SOPs well from your description; you test and refine them with the people who use them.

The small-business stack

  • Customer relationship management (CRM): one place for every lead and customer, their history and next action — from a well-structured Google Sheet to dedicated CRM tools.
  • Messaging: WhatsApp Business with catalogue, labels (new lead, paid, delivered), quick replies and auto-replies.
  • Orders and invoicing: order forms, invoice templates or invoicing apps; mobile money payment confirmations recorded consistently.
  • Bookkeeping: daily recording of income and expenses; monthly profit and cash review.
  • Inventory (for product businesses): stock levels, reorder points and supplier lead times.
  • Scheduling: booking forms and calendars for service businesses.
  • Automation layer: Make or Zapier connecting forms, sheets, email and messaging (see the No-Code Builder Lab).
  • AI assistant: drafting replies, proposals, SOPs and analysis.
Reorder point formula. For stocked products: reorder point = average daily sales × supplier lead time (days) + safety stock. If you sell 12 bottles of juice a day, the supplier takes 4 days, and you keep 20 bottles as safety stock, reorder when stock reaches 12 × 4 + 20 = 68 bottles.

Customer service at scale

Build an FAQ from real customer questions; create response templates in your brand voice; set response-time targets; use labels to track open issues; and summarise complaints weekly to fix root causes. AI can draft replies and analyse themes; humans handle complaints, refunds and sensitive situations with empathy.

Quality control

Define what "good" means for each product or service — checklists, photos of standards, tasting or testing steps — and check before delivery. Track defects or complaints per hundred orders. Consistency builds reputation faster than occasional brilliance.

Measuring operations

Key operational metrics include response time, order fulfilment time, on-time delivery rate, error or complaint rate, repeat purchase rate and cost per order. Review weekly and improve one process each month.

Avoiding over-engineering

Do not build complex systems before you need them. Start with the simplest tool that works, automate the most frequent and painful steps first, and upgrade as volume justifies it. A clear checklist often beats an expensive system nobody uses.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my operations designer. I will describe my business and how orders flow today. Map my process from inquiry to follow-up, identify the three biggest bottlenecks or error points, draft SOP checklists for the two most important steps, recommend the simplest tool stack for my size, and propose two automations with triggers and actions. If I sell stock, calculate reorder points from figures I provide.

📚 Glossary

  • CRM: customer relationship management
  • Reorder point: stock level that triggers a new order
  • Safety stock: extra inventory buffer against uncertainty
  • Lead time: time between ordering and receiving supplies
  • Fulfilment time: time from order to delivery

📖 References

  • Gerber, M. The E-Myth Revisited — systematising the business.
  • Slack, N. et al. Operations Management.
  • WhatsApp Business — labels, quick replies and catalogue documentation.

quiz.q: A juice seller in Limbe sells 12 bottles a day. The supplier takes 4 days to deliver, and she keeps 20 bottles as safety stock. At what stock level should she reorder?
opts: 48 bottles, since 12 x 4 = 48
80 bottles, since (12 + 8) x 4 = 80
68 bottles, since 12 x 4 + 20 = 68
36 bottles, since 12 x (4 - 1) = 36
quiz.x: Reorder point = daily sales x lead time + safety stock = 48 + 20 = 68. Omitting safety stock gives 48, which leaves no buffer.

quiz.q: Hermine wants to buy a CRM subscription because orders keep getting lost. Her processes from inquiry to follow-up are not written down. What does the module recommend first?
opts: Automate payment reminders first, as they cause the most errors
Document each step as a checklist first, then pick a tool to support it
Buy the CRM now, since tools enforce good processes on their own
Hire an operations manager and let that person choose the tools
quiz.x: Start with processes, not tools: map steps and write SOPs. Buying a tool first risks an expensive system nobody uses.

quiz.q: A Douala electronics shop's WhatsApp has 300 unsorted chats. Which feature from the module most directly helps track order status?
opts: QR codes added to flyers, business cards and receipts
Status updates posted daily with new products and offers
Broadcast lists that send promotions to saved contacts
Labels such as new lead, paid and delivered on each chat
quiz.x: Labels mark where each customer is in the process. Broadcasts and Status are marketing tools.

quiz.q: A US cleaning startup records 6 complaints in 150 jobs last month. What is its complaint rate per hundred orders?
opts: 4 complaints per hundred, since 6 / 150 x 100 = 4
6 complaints per hundred, since six were recorded overall
2.5 complaints per hundred, since 150 / 6 / 10 = 2.5
25 complaints per hundred, since 150 / 6 = 25
quiz.x: 6 / 150 x 100 = 4 per hundred orders. Inverting the ratio gives 25, which is orders per complaint.

quiz.q: Pierre, a Bafoussam caterer, wants an automation for 5 orders a week and a complex inventory system. What does the 'avoid over-engineering' principle suggest?
opts: Build the full system now, before volume grows beyond his capacity
Copy the stack used by a large hotel so he is ready for future growth later on
Avoid automation, since five orders a week is too few to need tools
Use a simple checklist and sheet, automating frequent pain points first
quiz.x: Start with the simplest tool that works and automate the most frequent, painful steps; upgrade as volume justifies it. Avoiding tools entirely misses easy wins.

quiz.q: A boutique uses AI to draft replies. A customer writes angrily demanding a refund for a damaged dress. How should this be handled according to the module?
opts: A human handles it with empathy; AI may help summarise the issue
Send the AI draft immediately to keep the response time short
Add the customer to a broadcast list for future discount offers
Use an automated refund rule so no staff time is spent on it
quiz.x: AI drafts and analyses themes; humans handle complaints, refunds and sensitive situations with empathy.

quiz.q: A bakery delivers 180 of 200 orders on time in a month. What is the on-time delivery rate, and how should the owner use it?
opts: 20%; report it annually to investors as a growth indicator
11%; compare it with competitors' advertised delivery rates
90%; review it weekly and improve one process each month
90%; recalculate it once a year when closing the accounts
quiz.x: 180 / 200 = 90%. The module recommends reviewing operational metrics weekly and improving one process per month.

quiz.q: A Kenyan agrifood startup sells 30 sacks a day, supplier lead time is 6 days, and safety stock is 40 sacks. Stock is now 210 sacks. Should it reorder today?
opts: No, since 210 is above the reorder point of 180 sacks
Yes, since 210 is below the reorder point of 220 sacks
No, since 210 is above the reorder point of 190 sacks
Yes, since 210 is below the reorder point of 240 sacks
quiz.x: 30 x 6 + 40 = 220; 210 is below, so reorder. Forgetting safety stock gives 180 and a wrong 'no'.

quiz.q: Comfort's tailoring workshop delivers inconsistent hem quality. Which quality-control step from the module best addresses this?
opts: Post more testimonials so customers remember the good orders
Define 'good' with a checklist and photos, and check before delivery
Automate order confirmations so customers know their delivery dates in advance
Offer a discount on the next order whenever a hem is uneven
quiz.x: Quality control means defining standards with checklists or photos and checking before delivery. Discounts treat symptoms, not causes.

quiz.q: An online store links its order form to a Google Sheet and an email confirmation via Zapier. Which layer of the small-business stack is this?
opts: The automation layer, connecting forms, sheets and messaging
The bookkeeping layer, since every order is recorded in a sheet
The scheduling layer, since orders include a delivery date
The CRM layer, since it stores each lead's history and actions
quiz.x: Make or Zapier connecting forms, sheets, email and messaging form the automation layer.

facts.t: Reorder point: 12/day × 4-day lead time + 20 safety stock.
facts.more: Reorder point = average daily sales × supplier lead time + safety stock. Below this level, you risk running out before the next delivery arrives.

facts.t: Core flow: inquiry, quote, order, payment, delivery, follow-up.
facts.more: Mapping operations from the customer's point of view shows where orders get lost or delayed — before you choose any tool.

facts.t: Track complaints or defects per hundred orders.
facts.more: A rate, not a raw count, shows whether quality is improving as volume grows.

facts.t: Improve one process each month.
facts.more: Small, steady improvements beat a big system nobody uses. Start with the most frequent, most painful step.

modules.d: Choosing the right money, building an honest, compelling pitch, and preparing for due diligence.
modules.body:
Not all money is good money

Funding should match your business's stage and model. Many successful small businesses never raise outside capital; they grow from profits. Others need external money to buy equipment, stock or reach scale faster. Raising money takes time, gives up control or adds repayment obligations — so choose deliberately.

Funding options

  • Bootstrapping: growing from personal savings and customer revenue — maximum control, slower growth.
  • Customer financing: deposits, pre-orders and subscriptions paid in advance.
  • Savings groups: njangi/tontines providing rotating access to capital.
  • Microfinance and bank loans: require repayment with interest, usually collateral or guarantees and good records.
  • Grants and competitions: non-repayable funds from foundations, governments and development programmes — for example the Tony Elumelu Foundation Entrepreneurship Programme, which has provided seed capital and training to African entrepreneurs. Competitive and requiring strong applications.
  • Angel investors: individuals investing their own money, often with mentorship, in exchange for equity or convertible instruments.
  • Venture capital: professional funds investing in businesses with potential for very rapid, large-scale growth — suitable for a minority of businesses.
  • Revenue-based financing: repayment as a percentage of revenue, available in some markets.
Equity is expensive. Selling 20% of your company for 5 million CFA values it at 25 million CFA after the investment (post-money valuation). If the company later becomes worth 500 million CFA, that 20% is worth 100 million. Only give equity to partners who add value beyond money, and understand every term you sign — seek legal advice.

The pitch deck

A strong pitch tells a clear story in about 10–15 slides: problem (who suffers and how much), solution (your offer and why it works), why now, market (bottom-up sizing), traction (customers, revenue, growth, retention), business model (how you make money and unit economics), competition and differentiation, go-to-market, team, financials (realistic projections with assumptions) and the ask (how much, for what, and what milestones it will achieve). Grant applications follow similar logic adapted to the funder's criteria, emphasising impact.

Using AI to build the pitch

AI is excellent at structuring your story, tightening language, designing slide outlines, anticipating investor questions, and building financial projection formulas from your assumptions. Ask it to play a sceptical investor and attack your pitch. But every number and claim must be true and evidenced.

Integrity in fundraising

Never inflate traction, invent customers, fake testimonials or present AI-generated projections as facts. Investors and grant panels conduct due diligence — checking records, bank statements, contracts, references and legal status. Misrepresentation destroys deals and reputations, and can constitute fraud.

Preparing for due diligence

Keep organised: business registration documents, financial statements and bank records, customer contracts or invoices, tax compliance, intellectual property, key agreements and team information. Good records also improve your own decisions — and are often the difference between businesses that receive loans and those that do not.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a sceptical investor and pitch coach. I will describe my business, traction and funding need. First, assess which funding sources fit my stage and explain the trade-offs. Then outline a 12-slide pitch deck, draft the problem and ask slides, build 3-year projection formulas from my assumptions, and list the 10 toughest questions an investor would ask. Flag any claim that needs evidence.

📚 Glossary

  • Bootstrapping: growing from personal funds and revenue
  • Equity: ownership share in a company
  • Post-money valuation: company value immediately after investment
  • Due diligence: investigation of a business before investing
  • Traction: evidence of market demand, such as revenue and customers
  • The ask: amount sought and its planned use

📖 References

  • Tony Elumelu Foundation — Entrepreneurship Programme (verify current terms).
  • Y Combinator — guides on pitching and fundraising.
  • Kawasaki, G. — 10/20/30 rule of pitching.
  • Feld, B. & Mendelson, J. Venture Deals.

quiz.q: Aisha sells 20% of her Douala logistics startup to an angel for 5 million CFA. What is the post-money valuation, and what is her investor's stake worth if the firm later reaches 500 million CFA?
opts: 5 million CFA; the stake would be worth 25 million CFA
25 million CFA; the stake would be worth 5 million CFA
20 million CFA; the stake would be worth 100 million CFA
25 million CFA; the stake would be worth 100 million CFA
quiz.x: 5 million / 20% = 25 million post-money; 20% of 500 million = 100 million. Subtracting the investment (20 million) gives pre-money, not post-money.

quiz.q: A Yaoundé hair salon earns steady profit and wants to add one chair. The owner is offered venture capital. What does the module suggest about fit?
opts: A grant fits better, since grants suit any business that wants to expand
Angel equity fits best, since equity is the cheapest form of capital
Bootstrapping or a loan likely fits better; VC suits rapid, large-scale growth
VC fits well, since any growing business benefits from investor networks and advice
quiz.x: VC targets very rapid, large-scale growth and suits a minority of businesses; a modest expansion can grow from profits or a loan. Equity is expensive.

quiz.q: A founder in Atlanta asks AI to produce 3-year projections, then puts them in his deck as 'expected results' with no assumptions shown. What is the problem?
opts: Projections must state assumptions; presenting them as fact misleads
AI cannot build financial formulas, so the numbers are likely to be wrong
Investors prefer 5-year projections, so the deck is too short
Projections belong in the appendix rather than the main deck
quiz.x: Never present AI-generated projections as facts; financials need realistic projections with explicit assumptions. AI can build formulas from your assumptions.

quiz.q: Marc runs a savings group (njangi) payout and also has customer pre-orders worth 600,000 CFA. He needs 800,000 CFA for stock. Which combination keeps maximum control?
opts: An angel investor for the full 800,000 CFA in exchange for 15% equity
A venture capital round, since stock purchases need professional funds
Pre-order deposits plus the njangi payout, with no equity given away
A bank loan for 800,000 CFA, leaving pre-orders for future marketing
quiz.x: Customer financing and savings groups keep control without equity or interest. A bank loan is viable but adds repayment obligations.

quiz.q: A grant panel asks Fatou for evidence of traction. Which item best counts as traction according to the module?
opts: A list of 500 social media followers who liked her launch post
A detailed AI-written market overview of the regional sector
A letter from a friend praising her drive and work ethic
Revenue records and repeat customers over the last six months
quiz.x: Traction is evidence of market demand such as revenue, customers, growth and retention. Likes are weak signals.

quiz.q: Before applying for a microfinance loan, Celestin has no separate business account and no invoices filed. What does the module say is likely to happen?
opts: Lenders focus on the pitch deck, so records matter little at this stage
Poor records make approval harder, since lenders check documents
Records can be compiled with AI after approval to satisfy reporting
Microfinance lenders skip due diligence for amounts below one million
quiz.x: Loans usually need good records; organised documents often separate businesses that get loans from those that do not.

quiz.q: A founder asks AI to act as a sceptical investor attacking her pitch. Why does the module recommend this?
opts: It anticipates tough questions so she can prepare honest answers
It writes the final ask slide so the amount sounds more convincing
It replaces the need for real investor meetings before raising money
It produces traction figures that make the deck look more credible
quiz.x: AI is excellent at anticipating investor questions; every number and claim must still be true and evidenced.

quiz.q: Which 'ask' slide best follows the module's guidance for a Cameroonian agri-processing startup?
opts: We seek funding to grow fast and become the leading brand in Africa.
We seek 15M CFA, and details on its use will follow after due diligence.
We seek 15M CFA for a dryer and 2 staff, to reach 40 tonnes by Q4.
We welcome any investment amount that partners feel comfortable with.
quiz.x: The ask states how much, for what and what milestones it will achieve. Deferring use details weakens credibility.

quiz.q: Ruth inflates her customer count from 40 to 400 in her pitch, planning to fix it later. What does the module say about this?
opts: Common practice, since investors discount every number anyway
Misrepresentation can destroy deals and may constitute fraud
A minor issue, since due diligence rarely checks customer lists
Acceptable if her projections show 400 customers next year
quiz.x: Inflating traction is misrepresentation; due diligence checks records and it can constitute fraud.

quiz.q: An angel offers 3 million CFA for 30% of a tutoring business. A second angel offers 3 million CFA for 15% plus mentoring from an education expert. Which is better per the module, and why?
opts: The first, since giving up more equity attracts a more committed investor
The first, since 30% equity means a higher post-money valuation
Both are the same, since the cash invested is identical in each case
The second: lower dilution and the partner adds value beyond money
quiz.x: Equity is expensive; give it to partners who add value. 15% implies a 20M post-money vs 10M for 30%, so the first offer actually values the business lower.

facts.t: Post-money valuation when 20% is sold for 5 million CFA.
facts.more: 5M ÷ 20% = 25M. If the company later reaches 500M, that 20% is worth 100M — equity is the most expensive money you can take.

facts.t: Slides in a strong pitch deck.
facts.more: Problem, solution, why now, market, traction, business model, competition, go-to-market, team, financials and the ask.

facts.t: Guy Kawasaki's pitch rule.
facts.more: 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point minimum font. A discipline for clarity rather than a law.

facts.t: Rotating savings groups — capital without interest or equity.
facts.more: Tontines give members turns at a pooled sum. They depend on trust and discipline and remain a key source of small-business capital in Cameroon.

labs.title: What does this money cost you?

A foundation's entrepreneurship grant

labs.tip: Every number and claim must survive a look at bank statements, invoices and references.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the first investor offer
plaibox.intro: Your Yaoundé packaged-snacks business makes steady profit. An angel offers money. Make each call: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.
plaibox.win: Strong judgement: you matched funding to need, protected ownership and kept every claim honest.
plaibox.lose: Review the funding options, the cost of equity and integrity in fundraising, then retry.

steps.s: You need 4M CFA for a sealing machine that pays back in 10 months from current orders. Which route first?
o: Sell 25% to the angel for 4M CFA
Values the company at only 16M and gives up a quarter forever for a short-payback asset.
Explore an equipment loan or supplier credit
Predictable payback suits debt — you keep full ownership.
Wait about two years and save it slowly from profit
Keeps control, but delays real, provable growth.

steps.s: The angel asks for traction numbers. Your best month was 2.1M CFA, the average 1.4M.
o: Present 2.1M as monthly revenue
Misleading — due diligence will expose it and destroy trust.
Show the monthly series with average and trend
Honest data builds credibility and invites a real conversation.
Say 'about 2M per month' and move on to the next topic
Vague rounding up still overstates and invites suspicion.

steps.s: The term sheet includes a clause you do not understand about future share issues.
o: Have a business lawyer review it before signing
Understand every term you sign — the module's explicit rule.
Ask an AI assistant to explain the clause, then sign it
Useful for a first read, but AI can misread legal terms; get advice.
Sign — the angel seems trustworthy
Trust does not replace understanding binding obligations.

steps.s: Before the meeting, AI produces a 3-year projection. What do you do with it?
o: Label assumptions and check each against real data
Projections are only as good as their visible, tested assumptions.
Present it as the company's forecast
Presenting AI projections as facts is misrepresentation.
Leave all financial projections out of the pitch deck
Avoids risk but investors expect realistic projections.

modules.d: Acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue — measured and improved systematically.
modules.body:
Growth is a system, not a campaign

Many businesses chase growth through occasional promotions. Sustainable growth comes from a system that consistently attracts, converts, retains and multiplies customers — measured and improved every month.

The AARRR funnel

Dave McClure's "pirate metrics" break growth into five stages:

  • Acquisition: how people discover you (search, social media, referrals, partnerships).
  • Activation: their first good experience (first purchase, first successful use).
  • Retention: whether they come back.
  • Referral: whether they bring others.
  • Revenue: how much value they generate.

Measure conversion between stages to find the biggest leak. If 1,000 people see your offer, 100 inquire, 20 buy and only 2 buy again, retention — not acquisition — is the problem.

Retention is the growth multiplier. Winning a new customer usually costs more than keeping an existing one, and loyal customers buy more and refer others. A business that keeps customers can grow steadily; one that leaks them must constantly refill a bucket with a hole in it.

Measuring retention

Repeat purchase rate: share of customers who buy again within a period. Churn rate: share of subscribers or regular customers lost in a period. Cohort analysis: track groups of customers who started in the same month and see what share remain active over time — revealing whether improvements are working. Net Promoter Score (NPS) asks how likely customers are to recommend you on a 0–10 scale; promoters (9–10) minus detractors (0–6) gives a score from −100 to +100. Sean Ellis's product-market fit test asks how customers would feel if they could no longer use your product; a commonly cited benchmark is that around 40% or more answering "very disappointed" suggests strong fit.

Growth levers

  • Referral programmes: rewards for customers who bring others — designed so both sides benefit.
  • Loyalty and subscriptions: recurring purchases and rewards for frequency.
  • Onboarding: making the first experience excellent so customers activate.
  • Content and community: educational content and groups that build trust and bring customers back.
  • Partnerships: businesses serving the same customers with complementary offers.
  • Pricing and packaging: bundles, tiers and upsells that increase revenue per customer.

Experimentation

Treat growth ideas as experiments: state a hypothesis ("A 10% referral discount will increase referrals by 30% in one month"), run it on a small scale, measure against a baseline, and keep or drop it based on results. Run one or two experiments at a time so you can tell what caused the change. AI can generate experiment ideas, draft messages and analyse results — the data decides.

Growth loops

The strongest growth comes from loops where customers' actions bring new customers: satisfied customers share photos of your product, which attract new customers, who share again. Design your product, packaging and service to make sharing easy and natural.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my growth analyst. I will give you my funnel numbers (people reached, inquiries, first purchases, repeat purchases, referrals) and monthly revenue. Calculate conversion between AARRR stages, identify the biggest leak, and propose three growth experiments with hypotheses, success metrics and baselines. Then help me design a simple monthly cohort retention table in a spreadsheet.

📚 Glossary

  • AARRR: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue
  • Churn rate: share of customers lost in a period
  • Cohort analysis: tracking groups of customers who started at the same time
  • NPS: Net Promoter Score: promoters minus detractors
  • Growth loop: cycle where customers' actions bring new customers

📖 References

  • McClure, D. (2007). Startup Metrics for Pirates: AARRR.
  • Reichheld, F. (2003). The one number you need to grow. Harvard Business Review.
  • Ellis, S. & Brown, M. (2017). Hacking Growth.
  • Reforge — growth loops essays.

quiz.q: A Douala clothing brand: 1,000 people see an offer, 100 inquire, 20 buy, and 2 buy again. Where is the biggest leak, according to the module's example?
opts: Activation, since 20 of 100 inquirers buy, a 20% conversion
Acquisition, since just 1,000 people saw the offer in total
Retention, since 2 of 20 buyers return, a 10% repeat rate
Referral, since no data shows how many customers refer others
quiz.x: The module uses this funnel to show retention, not acquisition, is the problem: only 10% buy again.

quiz.q: An NPS survey of 200 customers gives 110 promoters (9-10), 50 passives (7-8) and 40 detractors (0-6). What is the NPS?
opts: +55, since 110 out of 200 respondents are promoters
+60, since promoters plus passives minus detractors
+70, since 110 promoters minus 40 detractors
+35, since 55% promoters minus 20% detractors
quiz.x: NPS = %promoters - %detractors = 55 - 20 = +35. Subtracting raw counts gives 70, which is not a percentage score.

quiz.q: A Texas meal-kit startup runs a Sean Ellis survey: 28% of users say they would be 'very disappointed' without the product. How should the founder interpret this?
opts: Below the commonly cited 40% benchmark, so fit is not yet strong
Irrelevant, since NPS is the standard test for product fit
Strong fit, since over a quarter of users rely on the product
Strong fit, since the benchmark is anything above 25 percent
quiz.x: A commonly cited benchmark is around 40% or more 'very disappointed'; 28% suggests fit is not yet strong.

quiz.q: Ange wants to test three growth ideas at once: a referral discount, new packaging and a price rise. What does the module advise?
opts: Skip testing and adopt the idea her AI assistant rated most likely
Run one or two at a time against a baseline to see what caused change
Test them for one day each, since daily data is sufficient for decisions
Run all three together, since faster testing produces faster growth
quiz.x: Run one or two experiments at a time so you can tell what caused the change. Letting AI pick replaces data with a guess.

quiz.q: A Yaoundé gym has 200 members at the start of March and loses 16 by the end of March. What is its monthly churn rate?
opts: 16%, since sixteen members left during the month
12.5%, since 200 / 16 is about 12.5
quiz.x: Churn = customers lost / customers at start = 16 / 200 = 8%. 92% is the retention rate.

quiz.q: A bakery owner in Accra wants to know whether January's new loyalty card improved retention. Which method from the module best answers this?
opts: Compare total monthly revenue before and after January
Run a cohort analysis comparing customers by starting month
Count new Instagram followers gained since the launch
Ask an AI tool whether loyalty cards usually work well
quiz.x: Cohort analysis tracks groups starting in the same month to see whether improvements work. Total revenue mixes new and old customers.

quiz.q: Ange's Yaoundé bakery team is drafting growth experiments for next month. Which hypothesis is best written as a testable experiment?
opts: Customers like discounts, so we will offer some to everyone.
We will run several promotions and see what customers prefer.
Referrals will probably improve if we try harder with customers.
A 10% referral discount will raise referrals 30% in one month.
quiz.x: A good hypothesis states the change, expected effect and time frame so results can be measured against a baseline.

quiz.q: A Bamenda photography studio notices clients post photos with its watermark, which attract new clients who also post. What is this called?
opts: Churn, since old clients are replaced with new ones each month
A cohort, since clients arrive in groups that share timing
A growth loop, where customers' actions bring new customers
Activation, since new clients have their first good experience
quiz.x: Growth loops are cycles where customers' actions bring new customers; design sharing in.

quiz.q: A subscription tutoring service could spend 500,000 CFA on ads or on improving onboarding for new families. Its activation is poor: 40% of sign-ups never attend a first session. What does the module suggest?
opts: Spend on ads, since acquisition is the first stage of the funnel
Fix the first-session experience, where the funnel is leaking most
Spend on referrals, since referral is cheaper than any other lever
Split it evenly across all five AARRR stages to stay balanced
quiz.x: Find the biggest leak and fix it; with 40% never activating, more ads pour customers into a leaking funnel. Onboarding drives activation.

quiz.q: Two businesses each gain 50 customers a month. Business A keeps 90% each month; Business B keeps 60%. What does the module's 'leaky bucket' idea predict?
opts: A grows steadily; B must keep refilling and plateaus much lower
Both grow equally, since they acquire the same number of customers
B grows faster, since higher turnover brings fresh customers in
A plateaus first, since loyal customers buy less over time
quiz.x: Retention is the growth multiplier: B loses customers fast and must constantly refill. A loyal base buys more and refers others.

facts.t: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.
facts.more: Dave McClure's 'pirate metrics' (2007). Measure conversion between stages to find the biggest leak instead of buying more traffic.

facts.t: The range of a Net Promoter Score.
facts.more: % promoters (9–10) minus % detractors (0–6). Passives (7–8) count in the total but not in either group.

facts.t: 'Very disappointed' benchmark in Sean Ellis's product-market fit test.
facts.more: If around 40% or more of users would be very disappointed to lose your product, that commonly signals strong fit.

facts.t: Growth experiments to run at the same time.
facts.more: Run more and you cannot tell which change caused the result. State a hypothesis, set a baseline, then keep or drop.

modules.d: An integrated operating model for growing your business with AI — strategy, systems, numbers and governance.
modules.body:
Bringing it together

Your capstone designs your business's AI Operating Model: how the business will create, deliver and grow value over the next 12 months with AI integrated into strategy, operations and growth — and with the governance to keep it reliable and trustworthy.

Components

  1. Business snapshot: offer, customers, current revenue, team and key metrics.
  2. Market and positioning: bottom-up SOM, competitor map, positioning statement and target segments for the next year.
  3. Founder leverage plan: time audit results and the activities you will automate, AI-assist, delegate and keep.
  4. Operations stack: process map, key SOPs, tools and automations with owners.
  5. Growth engine: AARRR metrics with current values and targets, retention measures and three planned experiments.
  6. Funding plan: capital needs, sources and milestones; pitch outline if raising money.
  7. Financial model: 12-month revenue, cost, profit and cash flow projections with explicit assumptions.
  8. AI governance: approved tools, customer data rules, review steps for customer-facing content, and quality checks.
  9. Risks: key business and AI risks with mitigations.
  10. 12-month roadmap: quarterly priorities, milestones and the dashboard you will review weekly.
The one-page dashboard. Choose 6–8 numbers you will review every week: revenue, cash balance, new customers, repeat purchase rate, conversion rate, average order value, on-time delivery, and one customer satisfaction measure. If a number does not lead to a decision, remove it.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit your AI Operating Model (no more than eight pages), the financial model spreadsheet, and the weekly dashboard template. Present a five-minute pitch of your 12-month plan to your mentor or cohort, who will challenge your assumptions as investors or partners would.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my business model architect. Using everything I tell you about my business, draft an AI Operating Model with the ten components from this module in under eight pages, build a 12-month projection with explicit assumptions as spreadsheet formulas, and design a one-page weekly dashboard of 6–8 decision-driving metrics. Then challenge my three riskiest assumptions as a tough investor would.

Going deeper — capstone playbook: your AI Operating Model

Treat the capstone as a real management exercise, not a school assignment. The best operating models are short, numeric and honest about uncertainty: every target is tied to an assumption, and every assumption has an owner and a date when it will be tested.

Step-by-step timeline.

  • Week 1 — Diagnose. Complete the time audit, pull 3–6 months of actual sales and cash data, and write the business snapshot. Interview at least five customers about why they buy and what nearly stopped them.
  • Week 2 — Design. Draft positioning, the operations process map and the automation/AI-assist/delegate/keep plan. Build the 12-month financial model with a base, cautious and ambitious scenario.
  • Week 3 — Test. Run one automation or AI workflow live for a week and measure time saved and errors. Stress-test the cash flow: what happens if sales are 30% lower or a big customer pays 60 days late?
  • Week 4 — Finalise and pitch. Write the governance section, the risk register and the roadmap; rehearse the five-minute pitch and invite hard questions.

Deliverables checklist.

  • ☐ Operating model document (≤ 8 pages)
  • ☐ 12-month financial model with an assumptions tab
  • ☐ Weekly one-page dashboard template with current values
  • ☐ Evidence of one live-tested workflow (before/after time and quality)
  • ☐ AI governance page: approved tools, data rules, human review points
  • ☐ Five-minute pitch deck or outline

Assessment rubric (weighted).

  • Strategic clarity — 20%: clear customer, offer, positioning and priorities
  • Evidence and numbers — 25%: assumptions explicit, realistic and linked to data
  • Operations and AI design — 20%: workflows are specific, owned and tested
  • Governance and risk — 15%: data, quality and reputational risks handled credibly
  • Roadmap and dashboard — 10%: measurable milestones and decision-useful metrics
  • Pitch and defence — 10%: concise delivery, honest answers to challenges
Worked mini-example. A Yaoundé catering business serving office lunches finds the founder spends about 12 hours a week on WhatsApp orders and payment reminders. The plan: an order form feeding a shared sheet, AI-drafted daily menu posts reviewed by the founder, and templated mobile-money payment reminders. Live test: order handling falls from roughly two hours to forty minutes a day, with two order errors caught by a manual check. The model assumes three new corporate clients per quarter, tested by tracking proposals sent and won. The governance page bans pasting customer phone lists into unapproved tools.

Common failure modes.

  • A beautiful plan with no real numbers — or numbers with no stated assumptions.
  • Automating a broken process instead of simplifying it first.
  • Ten dashboard metrics that never change a decision.
  • Ignoring cash timing: profitable on paper, unable to pay suppliers.
  • Treating AI governance as boilerplate rather than rules people actually follow.

Submission and presentation structure.

  • 1. The problem and opportunity (30 seconds)
  • 2. Business snapshot and key numbers (1 minute)
  • 3. The operating model: positioning, systems, AI use (1.5 minutes)
  • 4. Financial plan and the three riskiest assumptions (1 minute)
  • 5. Roadmap, governance and the decision or support you need (1 minute)
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a sceptical investor and operations coach. Here is my business snapshot and 12-month plan: [paste]. List the five assumptions most likely to be wrong, tell me what evidence would prove or disprove each within 30 days, and propose a cautious scenario for my cash flow. Then ask me three hard questions I should be ready to answer in my pitch.

📚 Glossary

  • AI Operating Model: integrated plan for how a business creates and grows value with AI
  • Dashboard: small set of metrics reviewed regularly
  • Assumption: an estimate the plan depends on, to be tested
  • Roadmap: time-based plan of priorities and milestones

📖 References

  • Osterwalder, A. & Pigneur, Y. Business Model Generation.
  • Ellis, S. & Brown, M. Hacking Growth.
  • Forteh, I. (2026). AI Unlocked: Entrepreneurship. Team21 Academy.

quiz.q: Olivier's dashboard for his Douala restaurant lists 15 metrics, including social media likes he never acts on. What does the module advise?
opts: Keep all 15, since more data makes weekly reviews more complete
Replace them with one revenue figure, reviewed once a quarter
Ask AI to review the dashboard so he can skip weekly meetings
Choose 6-8 decision-driving numbers and drop those he doesn't use
quiz.x: Choose 6-8 numbers reviewed weekly; if a number does not lead to a decision, remove it.

quiz.q: A New York founder's capstone covers growth, funding and financials but has no rules on which AI tools staff can use or how customer data is handled. Which component is missing?
opts: The market and positioning section, with SOM and competitors
The founder leverage plan, listing activities to automate or keep
The governance section on approved use, privacy and review steps
The operations stack, including SOPs and automation owners
quiz.x: AI governance covers approved tools, customer data rules, review steps and quality checks.

quiz.q: Agnes's 12-month financial model shows revenue doubling every quarter, but the assumptions are not written anywhere. What will a mentor acting as an investor most likely challenge?
opts: The use of formulas rather than manually typed figures
The spreadsheet's layout and colour choices in the summary tab
The hidden assumptions behind growth, which must be explicit
The length of the model, which should cover three years
quiz.x: The capstone requires projections with explicit assumptions; mentors challenge assumptions as investors would.

quiz.q: A Bafoussam agribusiness founder writes a 14-page AI Operating Model. What does the capstone brief require?
opts: Cut it to a two-page summary and drop the financial spreadsheet
No change, since a longer document shows more thorough analysis
Add appendices so the main body stays at fourteen pages
Cut it to eight pages or fewer, plus the model and dashboard
quiz.x: Submit the AI Operating Model (no more than eight pages), the financial model spreadsheet and the weekly dashboard template.

quiz.q: Which pair of metrics from the module's suggested dashboard best tracks whether customers come back and are satisfied?
opts: Conversion rate and on-time delivery, reviewed monthly
Repeat purchase rate and a customer satisfaction measure
Revenue and cash balance, reviewed together each week
New customers and average order value, reviewed weekly
quiz.x: Repeat purchase rate and satisfaction directly reflect retention and experience. Revenue and cash measure financial health.

quiz.q: A Kigali founder's growth engine section lists AARRR stages but no current values or targets. Why is this a weakness?
opts: Without baselines and targets, progress cannot be measured
Targets belong in the funding plan rather than growth engine
AARRR is outdated, so the section should use NPS alone
Investors prefer funnels with three stages rather than five
quiz.x: The growth engine needs AARRR metrics with current values and targets, retention measures and three planned experiments.

quiz.q: Ibrahim's risk section lists 'competition' but no mitigation. Which revision fits the capstone best?
opts: New rivals may undercut us; we will lock in 12-month contracts.
Competition is high; we will work harder than everyone else.
Competition exists in every market, so no action is needed now.
Competition is a risk; AI will monitor it automatically for us.
quiz.x: The capstone requires key risks with mitigations; a specific action like contracts mitigates undercutting.

quiz.q: A capstone's roadmap lists 'grow the business' for every quarter. What does the module expect instead?
opts: Monthly social media themes, since growth comes from content
A five-year vision, since 12 months is too short for planning
Quarterly priorities and milestones linked to a weekly dashboard
A single annual revenue target, with quarterly reviews dropped
quiz.x: The 12-month roadmap needs quarterly priorities, milestones and the dashboard reviewed weekly.

quiz.q: During her five-minute capstone pitch, Rita's mentor challenges her 25% monthly growth assumption. What is the best response?
opts: Insist on the figure, since confidence persuades investors
Show the evidence behind it and a conservative scenario
Remove all growth assumptions so none can be challenged
Explain that an AI tool calculated it, so it is reliable
quiz.x: Mentors challenge assumptions as investors would; evidence and a conservative case show rigour. AI output is not evidence.

quiz.q: A founder's founder-leverage plan shows she will automate invoicing and delegate deliveries but keep client negotiations. How does this connect to entx1 Module 1?
opts: It contradicts Module 1, which says negotiations should be delegated
It belongs in AI governance, since it lists tools staff may use
It replaces the time audit, since the capstone covers those decisions
It applies the time-audit categories: automate, assist, delegate, keep
quiz.x: The founder leverage plan uses time audit results and the automate/AI-assist/delegate/keep categories; negotiations stay human.

facts.t: Components of the AI Operating Model capstone.
facts.more: Snapshot, market, founder leverage, operations, growth engine, funding, financial model, AI governance, risks and 12-month roadmap.

facts.t: Numbers on the weekly one-page dashboard.
facts.more: Revenue, cash, new customers, repeat rate, conversion, order value, on-time delivery and one satisfaction measure. If a number leads to no decision, remove it.

facts.t: Maximum length of the capstone document.
facts.more: Constraint forces clarity. Detail lives in the financial model and dashboard template you submit alongside.

facts.t: Length of the 12-month plan pitch to your mentor or cohort.
facts.more: Reviewers challenge assumptions as investors would — the riskiest assumptions should already be named in your plan.

labs.title: Which capstone component?
labs.intro: A founder drafted these lines for her AI Operating Model. File each under the right component.
items: Invoice reminders move to an automation; proposals become AI-assisted
The founder keeps all negotiations with corporate clients
Only approved tools; no customer phone numbers in free chatbots
Every customer-facing AI message is reviewed before sending
Repeat rate is 18%; target 30% by Q3 through a loyalty bundle
Experiment: referral discount for both friends
Revenue grows 5% a month, assumption: two new corporate clients a quarter
Cash flow shows a gap in August before school-fee season
labs.tip: Each component answers a different question; a strong plan links them with consistent numbers.

labs.title: Review this dashboard and governance draft
labs.intro: Tap every line that weakens the operating model.
segments: Weekly dashboard: revenue, cash balance, new customers, repeat rate,
conversion rate, on-time delivery,
Instagram follower count, total likes, page views, website hits, app downloads,
Vanity metrics that rarely lead to a decision — and the list exceeds 6–8 numbers.
and one satisfaction measure.
AI governance: the team may use any AI tool they like with customer data.
No approved-tools or data rules — exposes customer data.
Customer-facing AI replies are sent automatically without review to save time.
Errors at scale: customer-facing content needs a human review step.
Risk: our main supplier fails; mitigation: a second supplier qualified by June.
Our 12-month plan assumes no competitor will react.
Untested, risky assumption — exactly what reviewers will challenge.
labs.tip: Fewer numbers, explicit rules, human review, and assumptions you name and test.

plaibox.title: AI Operating Model prompt builder
plaibox.intro: Fill in your real business facts. The prompt asks AI to draft your operating model — then you check every number against your records.

fields.label: Business snapshot: offer, customers, revenue, team
fields.ph: e.g. catering for corporate events in Douala; 22 clients; 1.8M CFA/month; 4 staff

fields.label: Market & positioning (SOM, competitors)
fields.ph: e.g. SOM 60M CFA in Akwa/Bonanjo; 3 direct competitors; we are fastest

fields.label: Founder leverage: what you'll automate, AI-assist, delegate, keep
fields.ph: e.g. automate reminders; AI-assist proposals; delegate delivery; keep negotiations

fields.label: AI governance rules
fields.ph: e.g. approved tools only; no customer data in free tools; human review

fields.label: Riskiest assumptions
fields.ph: e.g. two new corporate clients per quarter

checks.label: Market section mentions SOM or competitors
Leverage plan uses the four labels

plaibox.tip: Now open your spreadsheet and confirm every number the AI used.
